title: Lumbini Sacred Garden: A Visitor's Guide
meta_description: How to visit Lumbini's Sacred Garden: the Maya Devi Temple and marker stone, the Ashoka pillar, Puskarini pond, best hours, tickets and etiquette.
summary: The Sacred Garden is the heart of Lumbini: the Maya Devi Temple over the excavated birth site, the Ashoka pillar of 249 BCE, the Puskarini pond and the bodhi tree. Give it at least two visits, one at dawn and one at dusk, remove shoes at the temple and allow two to three hours each time.

sections.heading: What the Sacred Garden is
paras: The Sacred Garden is the small, walled area at the southern end of the Lumbini development zone where Buddhist tradition, an emperor's inscription and modern archaeology all point to the same spot: the birthplace of Siddhartha Gautama, who became the Buddha. It sits in Rupandehi district on the plains of southern Nepal, at about 110 m above sea level, 22 km west of Bhairahawa and a few kilometres from the Indian border. UNESCO inscribed Lumbini as a World Heritage Site in 1997.

Everything most visitors photograph lies within a short walk: the white Maya Devi Temple, the Ashoka pillar beside it, the square Puskarini pond, a large bodhi tree hung with prayer flags, and the brick foundations of stupas and monasteries built here over roughly 1,500 years. Beyond the garden's boundary stretches the rest of the planned zone, with its canal and international monasteries, which we cover in a separate guide.

The garden is not grand. Expect brick, grass, trees and quiet. Its power comes from what it marks and from the people who come: Sri Lankan families in white, Tibetan monks with prayer beads, Thai and Vietnamese pilgrim groups chanting together, Nepali schoolchildren, and Indian families on day trips across the border.

The site has had a long silence. The Chinese pilgrims Faxian, around 400 CE, and Xuanzang, in the seventh century, both described Lumbini, but over the following centuries it fell out of use and was overgrown. After the pillar was found in 1896, interest grew slowly. The turning point came in 1967, when U Thant, the Burmese Buddhist then Secretary-General of the United Nations, visited and pressed for the birthplace to be developed. The master plan by Kenzo Tange followed in the 1970s, and the Lumbini Development Trust, set up in 1985, still manages the site today.

sections.heading: The Maya Devi Temple and the marker stone
paras: The Maya Devi Temple is a plain modern building, opened in 2003, that protects the excavated remains beneath it. Inside, a raised walkway leads you around layers of brick foundations from successive shrines. At the centre, behind glass and a railing, is a marker stone found during excavations in the 1990s by Nepal's Department of Archaeology and the Japan Buddhist Federation, at the spot tradition identifies as the exact place of the birth.

Look also for the worn stone relief of Maya Devi, the Buddha's mother, standing and holding the branch of a tree with her right hand, the posture in which Buddhist texts say she gave birth. The relief is eroded by centuries of devotion, and you will see pilgrims leaving money, flowers and silk scarves in front of it.

In 2013 an international team led by Durham University with Nepal's Department of Archaeology reported traces of an earlier timber structure beneath the brick temples, dated to around the sixth century BCE, with an open space in the centre where a tree may once have stood. The finding fits the old story of a birth in a garden and was published in the journal Antiquity.

Shoes come off before you enter. Photography is not allowed inside the temple. The walkway is one-way and can be slow when large groups visit, so the hour after opening and the last hour before closing are the calmest.

sections.heading: The Ashoka pillar
paras: Just west of the temple stands the stone pillar raised by Emperor Ashoka of the Maurya dynasty when he came to Lumbini on pilgrimage in the twentieth year of his reign, around 249 BCE. The lower part is fenced and its inscription, in Brahmi script and a Prakrit language, is protected behind a railing.

The inscription says, in short, that the king came here himself and worshipped because the Buddha Shakyamuni was born here, set up the pillar, and made the village of Lumbini free of tax, paying only an eighth share of its produce. It is the oldest known inscription in Nepal, and the most direct evidence for identifying this place as the birthplace.

The pillar had been lost under earth and jungle for centuries before it was located in December 1896 by an expedition involving the German archaeologist Alois Anton Führer and Khadga Shumsher Rana, then governor of Palpa. Our guide to Ashoka's pillars in Nepal tells that story and the history of its two sister pillars near Tilaurakot.

sections.heading: Puskarini pond, the bodhi tree and the ruins
paras: South of the temple lies the Puskarini, a stepped, square pond. Tradition says Maya Devi bathed here before giving birth and that the newborn prince was given his first bath in it. Pilgrims walk around it and many sit on its steps to chant or meditate.

Beside the pond, a large bodhi tree, the sacred fig under which the Buddha later reached awakening at Bodh Gaya, is wrapped in strings of prayer flags. The ground under it is the most popular place to sit, and in the early morning you will often find a monk or a group reciting texts in Pali, Tibetan or Vietnamese.

Around the temple and the pond are the low brick foundations of votive stupas and monastery buildings, dated by excavators from the Maurya period to the early medieval period. They are easy to walk past without noticing; look for the rectangular cells of monks' rooms and the circular bases of small stupas.

sections.heading: Planning your visit
paras: Come twice if you can. Dawn is cool and quiet and you share the garden mostly with pilgrims; late afternoon has soft light and the evening lamps. Avoid the middle of the day from March to October, when the brick paths radiate heat and the temperature can pass 38 °C.

Foreign visitors buy an entry ticket at the gate; Nepali and SAARC visitors pay less. Opening hours and fees change, so check current status before you travel. Carry water, wear a hat, and choose shoes that slip off easily, because you will remove them several times. The garden has toilets near the entrance and small shops selling flowers, incense and butter lamps.

sections.heading: Beyond the garden walls
paras: North of the garden, the Eternal Peace Flame burns at the head of a long central canal. On either side lie the West Monastic Zone, with Mahayana and Vajrayana monasteries, and the East Monastic Zone, with Theravada monasteries. At the far northern end are the Lumbini Museum, the Lumbini International Research Institute and, just beyond, the white World Peace Pagoda built by the Japanese Nipponzan Myohoji order. The Lumbini Crane Sanctuary, home to sarus cranes, is close to the pagoda.

The whole planned zone is about 4.8 km long and 1.6 km wide, so most people cycle or take an e-rickshaw between sites. One full day is enough for the monasteries and the north end; a second day lets you add Tilaurakot or Ramagrama.

faqs.q: How long should I spend in the Lumbini Sacred Garden?
faqs.a: Allow two to three hours for one unhurried visit, covering the Maya Devi Temple, the Ashoka pillar, the Puskarini pond, the bodhi tree and the brick ruins. Ideally visit twice, at dawn and in the late afternoon, which means staying at least one night in Lumbini. Add a full day for the monastic zones and the Peace Pagoda.

faqs.q: What is the marker stone in the Maya Devi Temple?
faqs.a: It is a stone found in the 1990s during excavations by Nepal's Department of Archaeology and the Japan Buddhist Federation, deep in the foundations beneath the old temple. It lies at the point tradition gives for the Buddha's birth. Today it is protected behind glass and a railing inside the modern temple, and visitors view it from the walkway.

faqs.q: Can I take photos inside the Maya Devi Temple?
faqs.a: No. Photography is not allowed inside the temple, and guards will remind you. You can photograph the outside of the temple, the Ashoka pillar, the pond, the bodhi tree and the ruins. Ask before photographing pilgrims or monks at prayer, and never use flash near people who are meditating.

faqs.q: What does the Ashoka pillar inscription say?
faqs.a: In Brahmi script, it records that King Ashoka, in the twentieth year after his coronation, came in person and worshipped here because the Buddha Shakyamuni was born here. He set up a stone pillar and made the village of Lumbini free of tax, paying only one eighth of its produce. It dates to around 249 BCE.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for the Sacred Garden?
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign visitors pay an entry fee at the gate, with lower rates for Nepali and SAARC nationals. The fee covers the garden and the Maya Devi Temple. Fees and opening hours are set by the Lumbini Development Trust and change from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What should I wear to the Sacred Garden?
faqs.a: Wear loose clothing that covers shoulders and knees, and shoes you can slip off easily, since you remove them at the temple. Bring a hat, sunscreen and water from March to October. In December and January, dawn can be 7–8 °C and foggy, so a warm layer helps. Light colours are cooler and common among pilgrims.

faqs.q: When is the Sacred Garden least crowded?
faqs.a: The first hour after opening and the last hour before closing are quietest, and weekdays are calmer than Saturdays, Nepal's weekly holiday. The busiest times are Buddha Jayanti in April or May and the winter pilgrimage season from November to February, when large groups from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar and India arrive.

faqs.q: Can I meditate in the Sacred Garden?
faqs.a: Yes. Many visitors sit under the bodhi tree, on the pond steps or along the paths, and pilgrim groups chant daily. Choose a spot away from walkways, keep your phone silent and sit so your feet do not point at the temple or at monks. For guided practice, see our Lumbini meditation retreat.

faqs.q: Is the Sacred Garden accessible for wheelchair users?
faqs.a: Partly. The garden is flat and the main paths are brick or paved, though uneven in places. The temple interior is a raised walkway, and access for wheelchairs there varies. E-rickshaws can bring you close to the garden entrance. Tell us your needs and we will check current conditions and plan the route.
